title: We stopped using screenshots. Our product page runs the real software.
deck: Every system on our products page renders its actual interface as live motion — no screenshots, no video files. Here is the architecture, and why it changes how a studio sells.
excerpt: How J Supreme Tech replaced product screenshots with live, CSS-driven software interfaces that run in the browser — the architecture, the trade-offs, and the payoff.
author: J Supreme Studio

blocks.text: A screenshot is a promise you took once and hoped stayed true. We got tired of the promise drifting, so we deleted the screenshots and made the product page render the actual software.

If you open our [products page](/products), nothing on it is an image. The pipelines move. An invoice gets marked paid. The AI agent answers a question and the typing indicator blinks. It is all **live DOM and CSS**, rendered on the fly, on every visit — thirteen systems, one engine.

Marketing screenshots have three problems that compound over time. They go stale the moment the product changes. They are heavy — a handful of retina PNGs can outweigh the entire rest of a page. And they are dishonest in a small way: they show a frozen best-case, never the thing moving.

items: **Staleness** — the product ships weekly; the screenshot was taken in March.
**Weight** — five 2x PNGs can be 4–8 MB; the page they sell is 200 KB.
**Flatness** — software is motion, and a still frame throws the motion away.

blocks.title: The reframe
blocks.text: If the interface is just markup, the *most honest* and the *lightest* demo is the markup itself — running, not photographed.

Each product demo is a self-contained React component with its own little state machine. There is no backend call, no real data — it is a choreography. A shared `useScene` hook drives a deterministic timeline, and every system plugs into it.

The trick is that the *layout* is the real product layout, lifted straight from the live build and frozen as a presentational shell. So when the product changes, the demo is one import away from changing with it.

blocks.caption: Fig 1 — one timeline, thirteen presentational shells subscribing to the same beat

blocks.text: Anything that animates forever has to respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Every scene checks the media query and, if motion is reduced, renders the *final* beat statically. The page still tells the whole story — it just stops moving for people who asked it to.

blocks.title: The cost
blocks.text: Live demos are more code to maintain than a screenshot, and they can jank if you animate layout instead of transforms. Animate `transform` and `opacity`; never animate `width`, `top`, or `height` in a loop.

Beyond weight and honesty, there is a sales effect we did not expect: a moving interface reads as *built*. A static one reads as *designed*. For a studio that ships working software, that difference is the entire pitch.
Show the thing running, or you are just showing a picture of a promise.

items: For a product studio selling working systems — yes, without hesitation.
For a brochure site that changes twice a year — no, a screenshot is fine.
The deciding question: does motion *prove* something a still cannot? If yes, build it live.

blocks.text: Want your product page to run the real thing instead of a picture of it?

faq.q: Does live software hurt page performance?
faq.a: Done right it helps — there are no image downloads, and CSS transforms run on the compositor. The risk is animating layout properties; we only animate transform and opacity.

faq.q: How do you keep the demos in sync with the real product?
faq.a: Each demo reuses the product's real layout as a presentational shell, so a product change is one import away from updating the demo.
